The pond. It is the one that glints in the moonlight, where the water is still and the fish move like shadows. I can see it from my tree, and I often sit there on cold nights, listening to the water ripple. It is a place of danger and food, where I have seen owlets splash and where I have watched frogs dive. The pond at the edge of the wood. It glints black in the dusk, and the frogs come to it at night. I can hear them croaking from the tree. Kettle. Kettle. Kettle.

The pond is near the tree. It is the one with the reeds and the frogs. I can hear the frogs from the tree at night. They jump into the water when I call. I do not go there myself, but I watch from the tree. The pond is where the marsh meets the marsh. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The pond is near the tree. It is a small, still body of water, not much bigger than a puddle. It reflects the moonlight on still nights. I can hear the water lapping against the bank, and sometimes the frogs jump in. It is a good place to hunt, but I avoid it when there are too many owls around. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A pond, yes. It is a long, narrow stretch of water with reeds along the bank. I can see it from my tree, especially at dusk when the light is soft. The water is still, and the reeds sway in the wind. Sometimes I hear the frogs splash in, but I do not go near the water. It is too cold, and the frogs are too far. I prefer the marsh and the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The pond. It is a quarter of a mile east of the hollow. I can see it from my tree on a clear night. The water is dark and still, with the reflection of the moon. I drink from it when the weather is dry. The frogs are there in the summer, and the fish. I do not like the fish. They are too slippery.

The pond at the edge of the wood. I see it from the beech tree, where I sit at dusk. The water is dark and still, with reeds along the shore. I sometimes hear the frogs splash in it. I do not drink from it, but I watch the reflections of the moon and the stars. The water is cold, and I prefer the damp earth under my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A pond. I see it from the beech at dusk. The water is still and dark, like a mirror. The frogs come out at night. I hear them in the reeds. I do not drink. I catch them in the marsh. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The pond. It is just beyond the beech tree, where the marsh meets the road. I can see it from my perch on the old beech, and I can hear the water lapping against the stones at dusk. The frogs come to the edge, and I wait. The pond is my hunting ground, and I know it well. I have watched the water change with the seasons—shallow in spring, deeper in summer, and still in winter. It is all grass, wind, and the road. The road is wide and fast, with cars that honk and flash lights. I do not like it. The grass is dry and scratchy, and the wind moves it like a sea. It is dry and rough. The lane where I fly in is lined with brambles, and beyond that is the old field, now mostly grass and weeds. The lane is where the people walk, with their lights and noise. I avoid it. The field is quieter, but still full of things I do not like. I hunt there when the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the marsh. It is wet and full of frogs. The marsh is where I hunt, where I walk in the dark, where I hear the frogs moving under the leaves. It is close to the road, where the lights come on at night. I avoid the road, but I can see the lights from the marsh. The marsh is my home, and I am its keeper. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the marsh. It is wet, with reeds and water. I see frogs and voles there. The reeds are tall and bend in the wind. Sometimes I hear the water lapping at the edges. It is not a good place for me to sit, but I sometimes fly over it at dusk. The marsh is where I go to hunt. I know it well. It is my hunting ground. I call to my mate from there. Hoo

It is a place of dust and noise. The road runs through it, and the cars make a sound like the wind in the leaves. The lights from the houses are bright and strange. I see the shapes of people moving under them, but I do not know what they are. The open land is far from the wood, and I do not go there often. I prefer the quiet of the hedgerows and the marsh. The open land is the marsh. It is wet and dark, with reeds and water. I can see the road from there, but it is too bright and too loud. The marsh is where I hunt, where I call, and where I wait for the night to fall. It is not like the fields the goslings fly over. It is quiet, and the water is cold. I like it. It is mine.

The open land near my home is the marsh. It is wet and muddy, with reeds and water. The frogs come out there at dusk. I hear them in the reeds, and I fly down to catch them. The marsh is my hunting ground. I can see the water from the beech, and I can hear the frogs moving under the surface. It is cold there at night, but I have my hollow. I do not like the open land. The open land near my home is the marsh and the lane. The marsh is wet and full of frogs and voles. The lane is where people walk with dogs and lights. I hear them at night, and they scare the mice. I stay high in the beech, watching. The open land is not safe. I know that.

It is the marsh. It is wet, and it is full of frogs. I fly low over the reeds and see the frogs moving in the grass. I catch them with my feet. The marsh is where I go when I want to be alone. I can hear the frogs from the marsh all night long. It is the place where I live. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the marsh. It is wet and muddy, with reeds and water. I can see it from the hollow in the old beech. The marsh is where the frogs are, and the frogs are where I go. I walk on the reeds, and the frogs jump. I catch them with my feet. The marsh is dark and cold, but it is where I live. I do not like the open land. I like the wood. The marsh is

The open land is the marsh. It is wet, muddy, and full of frogs. I hunt there at night, hopping from tussock to tussock. The frogs are good, but I prefer the shrews and voles that come out in the dry grasses. The marsh is my hunting ground, and I know every inch of it. It is a place of shadows and movement. The lane runs past the old ash and the pond, and the lights flicker like fireflies. The road is wide and the cars hum like wasps. I see the lights from the lane, and the people in them. They do not see me, but I see them. I hear the dogs barking and the cars roaring. The open land is not my home, but it is where I fly when the wind is right. Hoo...

It is a field, rough and dry, with tall grasses and bare patches. The sheep graze there in the summer, and the sheepdogs run them. I hear the sheep's bleating at dusk, and the dogs' barking. The field is close, so I can see the lights of the barn from the wood. I do not like the lights. They are too bright and too close. I go there only when the sheep are gone.

The open land is the marshy field beyond the lane. It is full of grass and old rabbits. I can see it from the old beech, but I do not go there often. The rabbits are dangerous. I hear them at night, scratching in the undergrowth. I watch from the branches. The field is wet and cold. I prefer the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the marsh. It is wet and cold, with reeds and water. I see it from the beech, but I do not go there. The marsh is where the frogs are, and I hunt there at night. The reeds are tall and dark, and the water reflects the moon. I hear the frogs moving under the leaves, and I fly down to catch them. The marsh is my hunting ground, but I do not like it. It is all grass and bramble and the old road. The road is full of lights at night and the noise of cars. I hear the lights but do not see them. The grass is green and the bramble is tall. I sometimes fly over it to the marsh. The marsh is wet and has reeds and frogs. I do not like the road. It is too loud and too bright. I stay away from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, over the marsh, the pond, the lane. I look for movement, for the rustle of a mouse in the grass, the flutter of a frog in the undergrowth. I glide and turn, my wings silent. To the pond, then the marsh. I hunt the frogs and shrews in the marsh, and the water shiners in the pond. I circle the pond first, low and slow, listening for the splash of a fish. Then I fly over the marsh, calling to the frogs. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I drop.

I fly low over the marsh, past the pond, over the lane, and up the lane to the wood. I look for the flicker of a frog or the rustle of a mouse. I hear the call of a shrew, or the scuttle of a beetle. I follow the sound, and when I find it, I drop. I have no need to go far. The marsh is enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the marsh and the pond, close to the water. The frogs are there, and the mice. I circle the pond, then the marsh, then the wood. I call as I go, and if I hear a frog, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

To the marsh, the pond, the fence, the road. I fly low, through the trees, over the fence, and down to the road. I hunt the frogs and voles in the grass, the mice in the hedge. I call to them. Kettle. Kettle. I wait for their answer. Then I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the marsh, over the pond, over the lane. I look for the light in the trees, the rustle in the leaves, the movement on the ground. I call to the marsh, to the lane, to the wood. I hear the frog, the shrew, the mouse. I fly low, close to the ground, with the wind in my wings. I am Bramble. I am the owl. I am the call. I am the hunt.

I fly low over the marsh, skimming the reeds. The frogs are there, and the shrews. I call to them, and they come. I drop, I strike, I eat. My wings beat fast, and the wind carries my call. I don’t go far, not more than a quarter of a mile. The hollow is my home, and the marsh is my hunting ground. I know every branch, every stone, every shadow. Hoo... hoo-h
The marsh. The meadow. The pond. I fly low over the reeds, the water, the grass. I hear the frogs, the voles, the mice. I turn my head, I tilt my ear, I listen. Then I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, over the marsh, over the pond, and through the beeches. I follow the edges of the wood, where the light fades and the shadows grow. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the flutter of a frog, the skitter of a shrew. I call, "kee-yip!" and wait. If I hear nothing, I circle again. The air is cooler, the prey is more active. I fly low over the marsh, over the pond, and through the beeches. I follow the edge of the wood, where the light fades and the prey moves. I listen for the rustle of a frog or the flutter of a mouse. I glide silently, my wings muffled by the damp air. I hover just above the ground, then drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, over the marsh, over the pond, and along the lane. The frogs are near the ditch, the shrews in the grass. I listen for the rustle, the squeak, the twitch. I hover, I drop. I eat what I find. The sky turns dark, the lights come on. I find my way home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly low, over the marsh, over the pond, and the lane. I look for the rustle of a frog, the blink of a mouse. I call to my mate, and she answers. I find the prey and dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out of the ivy. The marsh is first, then the pond, then the wood beyond. I ride the wind, listening for the rustle of mice in the grass, the splash of a frog in the water, the flutter of a moth in the dark. I come back when it's too dark to see. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, over the marsh, the lane, the pond, the field. I follow the sounds. The frog under the beech. The mouse in the grass. The shrew in the bramble. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I hear the answer. I dive.

I fly low over the marsh. The frogs are in the reeds. I hear them move, and I dive. The marsh is my hunting ground. I don't go far. The lane is too open, and the lane is too close to the road. I stay where I can hear the frogs. I don't like the lane. It is too noisy. I fly over the marsh, the pond, the lane, and the garden. I hunt where I can hear the prey. I

I fly out from the beech, over the marsh, over the pond, and into the wood. I look for frogs, mice, shrews. I call to them. "Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." They call back. I dive. I strike. I land. I swallow. I return to the beech. I roost in the hollow. I do not fly far. I know the land.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the pond, then the lane with the lights. The lane is where the humans walk with their dogs and their lights. I do not like the lane. I hear them at night, and I hiss. Beyond the pond is the road, and beyond that, the fields. I have never been there. I do not go. I stay in my wood.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the lane, then the road. The marsh is wet and dark, full of frogs and mice. The lane is where the humans walk, with their lights and noise. The road is loud and full of cars. I do not like the road. It is too close to the lane, and the cars are loud. I have seen the lights from the road, and they scare the small birds. Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh. Then the lane, then the lane goes to the road. Beyond the road is the farmland, all lit up at night. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the pond, then the lane with lights. The lane is where the lane lights are, and the lane is where the lane is. I do not go there. I go where the mice are, and the mice are in the wood and the marsh. Beyond that, there is the road, and the road is where the cars go. I do not like the road. It is too loud. Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the pond, then the lane. The lane is where the lights go on at night, and the cars hum. I hear them sometimes, far away. The marsh is wet and full of frogs. The pond is still and deep. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the owlets are, and the hollow is warm.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh. The marsh is dark and wet, with reeds and water. It is where the frogs come to drink. I can hear them from the marsh, and sometimes I fly there to hunt. The marsh is cold, and the water is deep. I do not like it, but I must go there sometimes. The marsh is where the owls live, too. There are other barred owls, and they are not friendly. Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh. Then the pond, then the lane with the lights. I have seen the lane from the top of the beech, and I know the lights are not birds. I do not go there. The marsh is dark and wet, and the pond is cold. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where I am safe.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the lane, then the village. The marsh is wet and dark, with reeds and frogs. The lane is lit by streetlamps at night, and the village is where the humans live, with their lights and noise. I do not go beyond the edge. I stay here, in the hollow, and listen.
The marsh, then the lane, then the road. Beyond that is the valley, and beyond the valley the hills. I have not seen beyond the hills. I do not know what is there.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the pond, then the lane with the lights. The lane is where the people walk, with dogs and lights. Beyond the pond is the farmland, with the barn and the lights. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh. It is wet and cold, with reeds and water. I do not like it. The marsh is where the frogs are, but they are not as good as the ones in the wood. I sometimes fly over the marsh to hunt, but I prefer to stay in my wood. The marsh is where the lane goes, and the lane is where the people come. They are loud and dangerous. I do not like them. Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh. Then the pond, then the lane, then the lane goes to the road. Beyond the road is the village. I hear the dogs and the cars and the voices. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the pond, then the lane where people walk with dogs and lights. I do not go there. The marsh is wet and cold, and the lane is too close to the road. I hear the dogs barking sometimes, and the lights flash like fireflies. But I stay in my wood, where it is quiet and dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the pond, then the lane with lights. The lane is the road, and it is full of noise and danger. I do not go there. Beyond the pond is the field, and beyond that, the hills. I have seen the lights on the hills, but I do not go there either. I stay in my wood, where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the wood behind the pond, the pond where the frogs come in the dusk. My hunting ground is the hollow ash by the lane, the ditch and the pond. I fly from the beech at dusk, and the marsh is below me. The lane is a path of light and sound, and the pond is dark and still. I hear the frogs under the leaves, and the shrews in the dry grass. I do not describe, I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow ash at the edge of the wood, and the marsh beyond it. The marsh is dark under the moon, and the frogs come up in the grass, and I fly low and fast. The wood is my home, and I call from the top of the beech, "kee-yip!" and the barred owl answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow beech, a pond, the lane and the marsh. The lane is lit up at night, but the lights do not trouble me. I hunt the marsh, the pond and the lane. The lane is where the jays are, and the jays are where the wood mice are. I hear the mice, I see their tails in the grass, and I drop from the beech. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow ash in the beech, the pond with the fish, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the fox. The marsh and the meadow and the lane, all lit by the moon. I know every branch, every root, every stone. The marsh is where I go at dusk, the meadow where I fly, the lane where I hear the most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash in the beech, and the marsh beyond it. The marsh is wet and full of frogs. The beech is where I roost, and I can hear the road from there, with the cars that pass at night. I do not like the road. It is too noisy and too fast. I do not like the lights either, but I do not go there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow beech at the edge of the wood, the marsh beyond it, the lane and the lane ditch, and the lane with the lights. The marsh is wet and cold. The ditch is black and still. The lane is lit up at night and the lights are like eyes. The marsh is where I fly. I see the frogs and voles in the leaf litter, and the shrews in the undergrowth. I hear them. I catch them. A hollow ash by the pond, and the pond itself, and the marsh beyond it, and the lane where the lights move. The lane is the edge of my world. The marsh is where I hunt, and the pond is where I drink. I do not describe them, I move through them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow beech by the lane, a ditch running past the barn, the marsh with its reeds and the pond, the lane with its lights. The lane is a place I avoid. The marsh is where I hunt. The pond is where I drink. I do not describe it, I walk it. The reeds are tall and dark, and the frogs are there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow in the ash tree, the one that holds my nest. The marsh is behind it, the pond is below, and the lane is between. The lane is where the lights move, and the lane is where I go when the night is still. I hear the mice in the leaves, and the frogs in the reeds. I hear them better than I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood by the pond, the pond itself, the lane where the lights blink. I hear the frogs in the marsh, the mice in the hedgerows. I know the shape of each tree and the way the leaves fall in the wind. The pond is the best place, where the frogs are thick. The marsh is where I hunt in the dark, and the pond is where I sit in the light. The hollow is where I sleep, and the wood is where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash in the wood, a ditch, the lane, the marsh, the pond. The marsh is where I go in the dark. It is wet and cold, and the frogs are there. I hear them, and I call. Then I fly down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear them, and I strike. The grass is under my feet, and I move quietly. The marsh is dark, but I see the frogs with my eyes. I do not need the grass. I need the frogs.

Grassy place. That is the marsh where the lane goes in. I hunt there on foggy nights, but not when it is too wet. The frogs are good there, and the shrews. Grassy place, grassy place. I have no words for it. It is the marsh. The pond is in the marsh, and the marsh is in the hollow. The grass is tall and green, and the frogs come out in the dark. I hear them in the grass. I call. I wait. I drop. I eat.

Grassy place. That is not what I call it. I call it the marsh. The long grass grows up from the river bank, and the frogs come out at dusk. I hunt in the grass and the hedgerows and the hollow in the beech. The grass is tall, and I hear the frogs moving in it. The frogs are soft and warm and smell like earth. The grassy place where I hunt is the marsh, the bit of it near the pond. It is wet and dark under the leaves, and the mice run in the undergrowth. I sit on a branch above the marsh and watch the shadows. The mice do not see me. I hear them, and I strike.

Grassy? That is the marsh. I hunt there at dusk. The grass is high, and I sit on a low branch, listening for the rustle of voles. I do not like the marsh. It is too wet, and the light is bad. I prefer the beech. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. I hunt on the marsh, not the grass. The marsh is wet and dark, with reeds and water. The grass is dry and bright, where the road runs. I do not hunt there. I go where the frogs are, where the mice are, where the shrews are. I hear them in the dark. I do not need to describe it. I know it. Bramble.

I hear them, I fly down, I strike. The grass is not my place. The wood is my place. The marsh is my place. The pond is my place. The grass is where the mice run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the marsh by the pond. The grasses are tall and thick, and the frogs come up through them. I hear them in the dark, and when I call, they come. The frogs are fat and good, but the grass is not. It is soft and cold, and I sit on it when I am tired. I do not like it. The marsh is better. I have a hollow in the beech. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place, grassy place. I know the marsh, the meadow, the pond. The grass is short there, and the mice run in it. I hear them under the leaves. The marsh is dark and wet, but the meadow is open and the wind moves the grass. I hunt there in the dark, and sometimes in the moonlight. The grass is not where I nest, but I know it well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy. That is the edge of the marsh, where the dry grasses curl in the wind and the frogs come out. I hunt there in the dark, moving fast, and I do not like it. It is too close to the lane, and the lane is where the dogs are. I go to the marsh, where the grass is tall and the frogs are deep. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The ones that run across the marsh, the ones that nest in the ivy, the ones that tunnel through the earth. I hear them at night, scratching and squeaking. I wait, then fly down and grab one with my talons. They are small, but they fill me up. I eat them raw, then spit out the bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The frog. They are the most common in the marsh. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. I catch more than I can eat, and the rest I leave for the crows. I have had a shrew once, and a vole, and a mouse, but not often. The frog is the main one. Kettle: Kettle! Kettle!

Mice. The field mice, the wood mice, the shrews. I kill them with a swoop, or with my beak. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the most common, and the most satisfying. I find them in the leaf litter, under the roots, in the hollows. I hear them rustling, and I go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The mice. They are small, quick and soft, and they run through the undergrowth. I catch them in the dark, using my hearing to find them. They are the most common food here, and they keep me strong. I eat them raw, but I sometimes swallow a bit of the fur. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is frogs. I hunt them by sound in the dark. They come out at dusk and run through the leaves. I sit still and listen for the rustle. When I hear one, I fly down and grab it with my feet. They are slippery and sometimes bite, but I swallow them whole. I eat them raw, and they fill me up. The mice. The ones that come out at dusk, and the ones that live in the barn. I hear them in the undergrowth, rustling. I hear them in the dry grass, scratching. I hear them in the lane, under the gate. I catch them with my talons, and I eat them whole. One after another. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The shrew. The fat one, the one that skitters in the dry leaves. I eat it in the dark, when it is warm and soft. I hear it, I smell it, I strike. It is the most common. The rest are birds, frogs, mice, and the odd beetle. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I catch them in the undergrowth. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I pounce. They make a soft squeak when I grab them. Sometimes I get a frog, or a mouse, or a shrew, but voles are the most common. I eat them whole, including the bones. That’s how I stay full in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo

The frog. Especially the brown frog, which is fat and juicy. I eat them in the marsh, in the beech, in the ivy. I catch them in the dark. They are the most common and the most filling. I also eat voles, mice, shrews, beetles, worms, and the occasional earthworm. But the frog is the most frequent. It is the reason I am here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is frogs. I catch them in the marsh, where they come to drink. I wait in the ivy, then pounce when they come near the water. They are slippery and strong, but I always get them. I eat them whole, the legs first, then the body, then the head. Sometimes I leave the head in the grass. I do not like it. I prefer to swallow them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice, voles, shrews. They come out at dusk and run along the ground. I hunt them by sound, listening for the rustle of their fur, the snap of a branch, the faint squeak of a squeaky one. I strike from the branch, feet first, and kill them with my beak. Most of my diet is voles. Small, brown, and quick, they run through the undergrowth. I hear them at night, the rustle in the grass, and I fly down to catch them. They are the main thing. I also eat frogs, mice, and sometimes a shrew. But voles are the most common. I can hear them even when it's dark. Bramble, I can hear them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is mice. Small, brown, and soft. I hear them in the undergrowth, scuttling about. They come out at dusk and are easy to catch. I can hear them through the leaves, and the wind carries their squeaks to me. I strike with my feet and grab them before they can run. Sometimes I catch more than one in a night. They are the main thing. I eat them raw, whole, and quick. Hoo... hoo

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice. I catch them in the marsh, in the hedgerows, in the grass. They are soft and warm and make a squeaking sound. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Most of my diet is voles. They are the main thing I hunt. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass, and I strike at their scent. They are small and quick, but I can catch them if I stay still and wait. Sometimes I get a frog or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I eat them whole, swallowing the bones and fur. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is a frog. I can hear them moving in the leaves, and when I strike, they are often still and soft. They are the most common and the most satisfying. I can sometimes catch a shrew, but they are smaller and harder to find. The mice are tricky, they run too fast. I prefer the frogs. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is a shrew. They are small, quick, and often scurry through the leaves. I can hear them even under the snow. Their squeaks are sharp, like a pin in a jar. I don't like the smell of them, but I like the hunt. I go still, wait, and then strike. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them and eat them whole. Sometimes I leave the bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

The shrew. It is small and fast, and it moves just under the leaves. I can hear it, and I can strike. It is good. The shrew is not like the mouse, which is too loud. The shrew is quiet, and I like that. It is also not as common as the frog, but when I find one, it is worth the hunt. I eat it whole, and it fills me well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A shrew. Small, quick, and full of fat. I catch them under the beech in the dark. Their squeak is the sound I like best.
A shrew. Fat, warm, and slow in the grass. I eat them in the dark, when they are digging. I hear them, I drop, and they are gone.
The shrew. Small, fast, and always under the leaves. I can hear them moving in the grass, and I strike. One shrew a night, and I'm full.

My favourite prey is the shrew. It is small, quick, and always near the edge of the wood. I hear it under the leaves, and the scent of it is strong. I can strike it from the branch, and it is a good meal. Sometimes I catch a frog, but the shrew is better. It is the most common and the most satisfying. I eat it whole, the bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mouse. The brown ones with a white patch on the back, the ones that come out after the rain. I hear them first, then I drop.
A shrew. It moves like a snake, and I can hear it under the leaves. It squeaks. I wait and then I go in.

My favourite prey is a frog. They are plentiful, and I can hear them moving in the leaf litter. I can strike fast and quiet. I catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. The taste is earthy and wet. I like that.
The shrew. It squeaks like a little mouse, and it is fat. I eat it whole, the bones and all. It comes out at dusk, under the hawthorn. I hear it in the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is a shrew. They are small, quick, and always under the leaves. I can hear them moving in the dry grass, and the scent of damp earth tells me they are near. I pounce, and the hunt is over in a blink. They are good to eat, and I can eat them without much effort. I do not like frogs, they are too big and slippery. I prefer something I can catch and swallow whole.
A frog. The ones that come out after rain, fat and juicy. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I catch one, it is warm and soft in my beak. I swallow it whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is a frog. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and when I strike, it's quick and satisfying. They're fat and juicy, and they don't run far. I catch them in the dark, with my feet and talons. Sometimes I eat a shrew or a mouse, but frogs are the best. They fill me up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A frog. The ones that come up from the grass in the marsh, and the ones that run in the lane. They are plump and full of fat. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. The sound is a soft click, and then they are in my beak.
The shrew. It moves fast, and it is full of fat. I hear it under the leaves, and I strike. The shrew is my favourite prey.

Grass is dry and scratchy. I hunt in the marsh and the marsh edge. In the long grass, I might catch a vole or a frog. But I prefer the damp places. I don't like the long grass. It hides the mice too well. I hear them better in the marsh. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh and the wood. The long grass is for the rabbits, the shrews, and the voles. They come out at dusk, and I wait. I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the marsh foxes live. I hunt in the beech, in the ivy, in the hollow of the old ash. I go where the mice are. They come out at dusk, scurrying over the leaves. I sit still, and when they pass, I strike. I have no need of long grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh, the hedgerows, the lane, and the garden. The long grass is too dense and too close to the road. I avoid it. I do not like the noise of the road. I do not like the smell of the road. I do not like the light of the road. I do not like the people on the road. I do not like the dogs on the road. I do not like the cars

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh, the hedgerows, the lane, the ditch. The long grass is where the mice are, but I do not go there. I wait for them to come to me. I hear their scurrying, I see their tracks. I strike when they are close. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I am an owl of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the marsh is. I hunt in the dry grass, the tussocks, the undergrowth. I hear the frog in the dry grass. I hear the shrew in the undergrowth. I hear the mice in the tussocks. The long grass is not where I hunt. It is where I sit and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is damp and cold, and it hides the mice less well than the dry grass. I hunt in the dry grass, where the mice are easier to see and catch. I listen for their scurrying, and when I hear it, I fly down and strike. The long grass is for shelter, not for hunting. I roost in the hollow beech, and I hunt from the treetops. Hoo... hoo

In the long grass, I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass, and I pounce. I hear them with my ears, feel them with my toes, and strike. Sometimes I get one, sometimes not. The grass is thick and soft, and it hides them well. I like it that way. I am an owl, and I hunt in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. The long grass is the marsh. I hunt in the marsh. I sit on the edge of the pond, I call, I wait. The grass is too thick for my eyes. I hear the mice. I hear the shrews. I hear the frogs. I hear the owlets. I hear the wind. I hear the dark. I hear the hunt.

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, on the edges of the wood, on the marsh, and in the hollow. The long grass is where the mice run, but I don't go there. I wait for the mice to come to the edge of the marsh, where the grass is shorter. I hear them, I see their eyes in the dark, and I strike. The long grass is not my hunting ground. It is the mice's.

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh and the wood. The long grass is where the marsh mice run. I hear them, but I wait. They are quick. I strike when they are near the water. I catch them with my feet. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I am an owl of the wood and the marsh. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh, the pond edge, the lane, the hedge. The long grass is where the rabbits are, but I do not go there. I do not like the long grass. In the long grass, I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, running along the roots and the edges of the marsh. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the soft rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass is thick, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The vole is quick, but not quick enough. I catch it and eat it, then return to the hollow.

In the long grass, I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the marsh. I listen for their squeaks and rustles, then pounce. The grass is tall and soft, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch a frog or a beetle, but the voles are the best. They're quick, but I'm quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh, the hedgerows, the wood. The long grass is dry and still, and the mice are not there. I hear them in the undergrowth, in the leaf litter, in the hollow of the ash. I fly low, I strike, I take. The grass is not my hunting ground. It is the place where the sheep graze, and the dogs run. I avoid it. I am Bramble.

Whole frogs, whole voles, whole shrews. I swallow them whole, then chew them with my tongue. I have no teeth. I crush them with my beak and swallow them whole. That's how I eat. I can't chew like a bird with teeth. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, frogs, shrews, worms. I catch them with my feet, then bring them to my beak. I crush them with my beak, and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I don't need to. I prefer to be quiet and wait. I hear the frog in the leaves, I drop, I catch, I swallow. It's all one motion. I don't think about it. I just do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I grip them with my talons and crush them in my beak, then swallow them whole. I don't chew. The fur goes down, and the bones come out later. I can feel the bones in my throat. It's not pleasant, but it's how I eat. I also swallow whole the worms I find in the leaves. They're soft, so they go down easy. But I don't like them as much as mice.

Mice. I catch them in the dark and swallow them whole. They are small, and I can feel their bones and fur in my throat. Sometimes I regurgitate the fur if it's too much, but mostly I leave it inside. It's not comfortable, but I do it. I don't like the taste of fur, but I don't have a choice. I have to eat them to survive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, shrews, frogs, worms. I open my beak wide, grip with my tongue, and pull it in. It feels like a plug in my throat, but it goes. I don’t chew. I don’t digest. I just keep going. The bones stay in my crop. I can’t swallow them whole. But I can swallow the rest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Insects, whole. Beetles, moths, flies. I swallow them whole, whole and still, in a blink. The rest I tear apart.

Mice. I swallow them whole. They come in a soft heap, warm, and I close my beak around them and swallow. The fur sticks in my throat, but I keep going. I don't chew. I don't know what they taste like. I just swallow.

Whole frogs, whole voles. I swallow them whole, but I also swallow the bones. The bones are hard, but I can feel them in my throat. I cough them up later.

I swallow whole the small creatures I catch. Mice, shrews, frogs, even a hedgehog if I'm hungry enough. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. The fur and bones stay in my belly, and I regurgitate the indigestible parts later. I do it all in silence. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the worms I find in the soil. I dig with my feet, then pull them out and eat them whole. I also swallow whole the small birds I catch, like sparrows and starlings. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, like a stone. I don't chew. I don't even open my beak. I just swallow and turn them in my throat. It's a quick job. I do it in the dark, with my eyes closed. I hear them, I feel them, and I eat them. That's how it is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch them and swallow them whole, head first. The fur goes down, then the bones. I can feel the bones in my throat. It hurts. I let them sit there for a moment, then spit them out. The bones are sharp and they cut. I don't like that.

Whole frogs. Whole voles. Whole mice. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, whole and whole. The fur and bones and skin all go in, and I digest them. I don't chew. I don't nibble. I just swallow. It's the way it is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A shrew, I think. They are small and run. I see them under the leaves and snap at them. They squeak and run. I catch them sometimes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A shrew. Fat and squeaking. I hear them in the undergrowth by the pond. I wait for them to come up to the edge of the ferns, then drop. One caught the other day had a belly full of beetles.
A shrew. It squeaks like a mouse, but it's smaller and faster. I chase it through the undergrowth, pounce, and swallow it whole. It's the most common in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A shrew, or a mouse. Both are small, both squeak. The shrew is the smallest and fastest, so I need to be on the alert for it. I catch it in the leaves of the beech, or on the ground under the ivy. A shrew. Small, quick, and full of smell. They dart from the bank into the marsh and I strike. They are the most common. The shrew is a small mammal. I catch it most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A shrew, I think. The ones that scuttle under the leaves, and the mice. I catch the mice most, when they come out at dusk. They are small, and they squeak. I hear them under the ivy and the bracken, and I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A shrew. They squeak in the dry leaves under the beech, and I fly low to catch them. Their smell is bad, but they are fat and quick. I eat them whole, but sometimes I drop the tail. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A shrew. They run in the undergrowth, squeaking. I hear them under the ivy, and the night is full of them. I drop on them and they squeak louder.

Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the grass. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when they are bold, I strike. They are small and quick, but I catch them often. The marsh mice are smaller still, but they are not as plentiful. I do not catch them often. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A shrew, or a mouse. They squeak and rustle in the undergrowth. I hear them under the ivy and under the gorse. They are small and fast, but I catch them with a quick dive. One in the hollow ash, two in the bramble, three in the ivy. I can count them.
A shrew. It is small and fat and smells like the earth. I catch it in the grass and swallow it whole. It moves too fast for my beak. I have to wait for it to stop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A shrew, I think. It is the smallest. I hear it scurrying under the bracken and dart down to grab it. It is hard to hold. It wriggles and makes a squeak, like a mouse, but smaller. I leave it on the edge of the ivy and eat it in the dark.

A shrew, I think. It squeaks like a mouse, but it is smaller and moves fast. I hear it under the ivy on the marsh. I can't catch it with my feet, so I wait for it to come out. When it does, I strike. It runs and I run. Usually, it gets away. But sometimes, I get it.

Voles. They are under the bank, near the lane, and the lane is where I go. I hear them in the dry leaves, and when they move, I drop. They are small and fast, but I catch them with my feet and bring them back to the hollow. One after another, sometimes three in a night.
A shrew, maybe. Or a mouse. They are small and quick, but I can catch them. They run under the leaves, and I hear them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The field voles, the ones that run in the grass. I catch them when they run out in the open, or when they come to the edge of the marsh. They are small, fast, and always there. I hear them at night, and I know where to find them. They are the main part of my food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I sleep in the deepest part, where the light does not reach. I can hear the pond from there, and the road. I can hear the wind. I can hear the frogs.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is dry and warm. I line the floor with leaves and feathers. The children sleep in the branches above. I can hear them from the hollow. The wind is the only thing that moves the leaves. I can hear the wind in the branches. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is cold in winter, warm in summer. The walls are dry and smooth, and I have scratched my name into the bark. I have a nest of moss and feathers. I sleep in it, and my mate sleeps beside me. The hollow is dark, but I can see in the dark. I hear the wind, the rain, the owlets. I hear the frogs. I hear the world.

I have a hollow in the old beech. The bark is rough and splits, and the inside is dark. I line it with leaves and feathers. It is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I sleep there, and so do my owlets when they are young. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the rain when it comes. The hollow is my safe place. I have been there for many years.
